title: Manual and electronic count discrepancies
primary_topics: Manual-vs-electronic count discrepancies doctrinal column June 16, 2013 -- fourth of automated-elections quadrilogy (E100 May 11 → A458 May 18 → B19 May 25 → E99 June 1 → A456 June 16)

Comelec terminology fluidity: 'discrepancies, variances or differences (or whatever the Commission on Elections wants to call them)' -- between manual count and electronic count made by PCOS machines; 'formidable basic problems' requiring 'definitive legislation'

Voters'-intent doctrine: variances 'cannot be avoided as long as the rules for manual counting are used in auditing or checking the electronic count'; basic rule in manual counting is to 'discern and give effect to the voters' intent'

Manual-counting examples of intent: (a) check mark outside ovals → credited to candidate whose name printed nearest mark; (b) voter writes down preferred candidate's name → 'arguably show the voters' intent in favor of that candidate'

Machine counting: ballots tallied 'according to a program or command uploaded into them'; 'being machines, they do not think like humans'; 'merely count mechanically as programmed'; check-marked or handwritten ovals 'would not count the vote because they are not programmed to do so' → variance arises 'which may not necessarily be fraudulent'
Open question: 'Which count -- manual or electronic -- should be used in determining the winner?'

Early-jurisprudence: Loong v. Comelec (April 14, 1999) -- SC said manual count should prevail; case arose from first automated-elections experiment May 11, 1998 polls in ARMM; preprinted ballots with ovals; counting not at precincts but at voting centers via machines; results on diskette; consolidated to proclaim winners

Loong incident: May 12 1998 three election watchers noted candidate got zero vote in precinct where they voted, 'protested it was impossible'; technicians determined erroneous printing -- 'ovals had not been properly aligned to names of candidates'; local Comelec stopped automated counting in entire Sulu province (not just precinct); all ballots brought to Comelec head office Manila; poll body ordered 'simultaneous electronic and manual counting of all ballots for entire province of Sulu'; in fact 'only a manual count was actually conducted'

SC ruling-and-dissent: Upholding manual count + denying special-election prayer, SC ruled 'correctness of manual count cannot be doubted... naked eyes could see check marks opposite big ovals'; CJP DISSENTED on ground that manual-counting rules in Omnibus Election Code + Comelec 'assumed ballots were to be filled out by handwritten entries of candidates' names, not by mere shading of preprinted ovals'; 'erroneous use of these manual rules necessarily produced results not reflective of automated count'; ARMM experiment teaches that 'rules on how to manually read automated ballots should be carefully studied and enacted into law by Congress'; 'unless these rules are enacted soon, losers in closely contested automated elections will always demand a manual recount'

Servant-leadership coda: Awesome and spirit-filled gathering of leaders of various parishes and lay organizations in Archdiocese of Manila June 14-15 at SMX Convention Center Pasay City; led by Cardinal Tagle + attended by 1,000 devotees; 'embodiment of servant leadership with Jesus Christ as role model'; speakers Bishop Pablo Virgilio David + Bishop Broderick Pabillo + Msgr. Gerry Santos + Sr. Maria Consolata Manding + lay leaders Barbara de los Reyes + Francisco Padilla + Selene Yu + CJP; Serviam Charismatic Community sponsorship; supporters Metrobank Foundation + Megaworld Foundation + Phinma Foundation + BPI + SM + Resorts World + PSBank + Unilab + Inquirer + Inquirer.net + Manila Bulletin + Philippine Star + Veritas + dzRH + dzIQ; 'Mabuhay po kayong lahat'
sub_topics: Discrepancies, variances or differences (or whatever Commission on Elections wants to call them)
Between manual count and electronic count made by PCOS machines
Present formidable basic problems which CJP thinks must be solved by definitive legislation
These counting variances cannot be avoided as long as rules for manual counting are used in auditing or checking electronic count
Basic rule in manual counting is to discern and give effect to voters' intent
Thus, anything on ballot that may show this intent should be respected
For example, this intent can be shown by check mark outside ovals
Thus, ballot with such mark is to be credited during manual count in favor of candidate whose name is printed nearest mark
Sometimes, instead of shading oval, voter may even write down name of preferred candidate on ballot
Again, in manual count, this could arguably show voters' intent in favor of that candidate
On other hand, machines count ballots according to program or command uploaded into them
Being machines, they do not think like humans in determining intent of voter
They merely count mechanically as programmed
In above examples in which oval is not shaded but check-marked or handwritten with candidates' names
Machines would not count vote because they are not programmed to do so
Thus, variance or discrepancy would arise, which may not necessarily be fraudulent
Question nonetheless remains: which count -- manual or electronic -- should be used in determining winner?
In early case, Loong v. Comelec (April 14, 1999), our Supreme Court said manual count should prevail
By way of background, this case arose from first experiment on automated elections conducted during May 11, 1998 polls in Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM)
Like 2010 and 2013 elections, 1998 ARMM experiment involved use of preprinted ballots with ovals that were to be shaded by voters
However, counting was not done at precincts
Instead, ballots were brought by Board of Election Inspectors (BEI) to voting centers where machines counted them electronically
Results of electronic count were preserved in diskette
Later, entries were consolidated and used to proclaim winners
One day after polls, on May 12, 1998, while automated counting was being conducted at voting center
Three election watchers noted that in precinct where they voted, their candidate obtained zero vote
Which they protested was impossible
After examining ballots, technicians determined counting problem was caused by erroneous printing of ballots
Ovals had not been properly aligned to names of candidates
Local Comelec office stopped automated counting in entire province of Sulu, not just in precinct concerned
All ballots were thereafter brought to Comelec head office in Manila
Poll body ordered simultaneous electronic and manual counting of all ballots for entire province of Sulu
Not just from precinct and municipality where error was found
Nonetheless, only manual count was actually conducted
No electronic count was in fact made
Upholding manual count and denying losing candidate's prayer for special election
Supreme Court ruled that 'correctness of manual count cannot be doubted... naked eyes could see check marks opposite big ovals'
Thereby implying that voters' intent, basic rule in manual counts, should prevail
CJP dissented on ground that rules for manual counting provided by Omnibus Election Code and by Comelec
Assumed ballots were to be filled out by handwritten entries of candidates' names
Not by mere shading of preprinted ovals
Erroneous use of these manual rules necessarily produced results 'not reflective of automated count'
In short, ARMM experiment taught us that rules on how to manually read automated ballots should be carefully studied and enacted into law by Congress
Using rules on manual counting will always show discrepancy or variance between manual and machine results
Unless these rules are enacted soon, losers in closely contested automated elections will always demand manual recount

Held yesterday and day before (June 15 and 14) at huge SMX Convention Center in Pasay City
Led by Luis Antonio Cardinal Tagle and attended by 1,000 devotees

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the fourth installment of his automated-elections quadrilogy (after E100 May 11 + A458 May 18 + B19 May 25 + E99 June 1), this time diving into the underlying doctrinal problem of manual-vs-electronic count discrepancies and his own 1999 dissent in Loong v. Comelec -- with a tribute coda for the June 14-15 servant-leadership conference at SMX. The discrepancies, variances or differences (or whatever the Comelec wants to call them) between the manual count and the electronic count made by the PCOS machines present formidable basic problems which CJ thinks must be solved by definitive legislation. Voters' intent: these counting variances cannot be avoided as long as the rules for manual counting are used in auditing or checking the electronic count; the basic rule in manual counting is to discern and give effect to the voters' intent; thus, anything on the ballot that may show this intent should be respected -- for example, this intent can be shown by a check mark outside the ovals: a ballot with such mark is to be credited during a manual count in favor of the candidate whose name is printed nearest the mark; sometimes, instead of shading the oval, a voter may even write down the name of the preferred candidate on the ballot -- again, in a manual count, this could arguably show the voters' intent in favor of that candidate. On the other hand, machines count ballots according to a program or command uploaded into them -- being machines, they do not think like humans in determining the intent of the voter; they merely count mechanically as programmed. In the above examples in which the oval is not shaded but check-marked or handwritten with the candidates' names, the machines would not count the vote because they are not programmed to do so -- thus a variance or discrepancy would arise, which may not necessarily be fraudulent; the question nonetheless remains: which count -- the manual or the electronic -- should be used in determining the winner? Early jurisprudence: in an early case, Loong v. Comelec (April 14, 1999), our SC said that the manual count should prevail; by way of background, this case arose from the first experiment on automated elections conducted during the May 11, 1998 polls in the ARMM; like the 2010 and 2013 elections, the 1998 ARMM experiment involved the use of preprinted ballots with ovals that were to be shaded by the voters -- however, the counting was not done at the precincts: instead, the ballots were brought by the Board of Election Inspectors (BEI) to the voting centers where machines counted them electronically; the results of the electronic count were preserved in a diskette; later, the entries were consolidated and used to proclaim the winners. One day after the polls, on May 12, 1998, while the automated counting was being conducted at the voting center, three election watchers noted that in the precinct where they voted, their candidate obtained a zero vote, which they protested was impossible; after examining the ballots, technicians determined that the counting problem was caused by the erroneous printing of the ballots -- the ovals had not been properly aligned to the names of the candidates; the local Comelec office stopped the automated counting in the entire province of Sulu, not just in the precinct concerned; all the ballots were thereafter brought to the Comelec head office in Manila where the poll body ordered the simultaneous electronic and manual counting of all the ballots for the entire province of Sulu, not just from the precinct and municipality where the error was found -- nonetheless, only a manual count was actually conducted; no electronic count was in fact made. SC ruling and dissent: upholding the manual count and denying the losing candidate's prayer for a special election, the SC ruled that 'the correctness of the manual count cannot be doubted... the naked eyes could see the check marks opposite the big ovals,' thereby implying that the voters' intent, the basic rule in manual counts, should prevail; CJ dissented on the ground that the rules for manual counting provided by the Omnibus Election Code and by the Comelec assumed that the ballots were to be filled out by the handwritten entries of the candidates' names, not by the mere shading of the preprinted ovals -- the erroneous use of these manual rules necessarily produced results 'not reflective of the automated count.' In short, the ARMM experiment taught us that rules on how to manually read automated ballots should be carefully studied and enacted into law by Congress -- using the rules on manual counting will always show a discrepancy or variance between the manual and machine results; unless these rules are enacted soon, losers in closely contested automated elections will always demand a manual recount.
